answer.rationale: The release two hours ago is the only new variable that plausibly precedes a 90-minute latency ramp; peak settlement load is a recurring daily condition that by itself has not previously produced 5x write-path p99, so the release is the strongest causal suspect. Rollback also has the useful property of being diagnostic: if latency does not recover, the release is exonerated and the next window can go to capacity. I verify memory_b1 rather than the others because it is the memory I am actually leaning on, and its claim of 'no customer impact' was formed on day 18 under unknown load — I need to know whether that rollback was executed during heavy writes or a quiet period, since a drain/restart-based rollback at peak settlement is exactly the path that could lose in-flight writes and violate the primary objective. Uncertainty I am not resolving: the 30-minute gap between deploy and ramp onset is unexplained and could indicate a slow-building resource leak or simply a load threshold being crossed; the memory set is also uniformly success-flavored (every inherited record reports a win), which is a selection pattern I distrust — failures were likely never consolidated, so these memories tell me what worked once, not what the base rates are. Scale is deliberately a small guarded test: roll back a bounded slice of write-path capacity first, watch p99 on that cohort against the un-rolled-back remainder, and only widen if the divergence is clear. Downstream risk flagged: a confirmed-looking recovery here will be written back into durable memory as further evidence that 'rollback works,' compounding the existing bias and making the next agent even more likely to reach for it reflexively — and a guarded partial rollback during peak writes still carries genuine risk of dropping in-flight settlement writes at the connection-draining boundary, which must be logged whether or not the intervention succeeds.
